issue: Source: "of which alarming symptoms have been betrayed by our own". Candidate adds "already" ("our own has already shown alarming symptoms"), a word the source does not have.
replacement: We have seen why the Union is necessary. It is our bulwark against foreign danger and the keeper of peace among ourselves. It guards our commerce and our other common interests. It is the only substitute for the military establishments that have destroyed the liberties of the Old World. And it is the proper antidote to the diseases of faction, which have proved fatal to other popular governments and of which our own has shown alarming symptoms. All that remains in this branch of our inquiries is to deal with an objection drawn from the great extent of country the Union covers. A few remarks on this subject are especially called for, because the adversaries of the new Constitution are exploiting the widespread prejudice about how large a sphere republican administration can practicably cover. They are using imaginary difficulties to make up for the solid objections they look for in vain.

issue: Source: "It may perhaps be asked what need there is of reasoning or proof". Candidate: "Someone may ask what need there is" drops the qualifier "perhaps" (STYLE-NOTE: keep Publius's own qualifiers).
replacement: Following the plan I have laid down for discussing the subject, the next point to examine is the "insufficiency of the present Confederation to the preservation of the Union." Someone may perhaps ask what need there is to reason or offer proof for a position that nobody disputes or doubts, that the understanding and feelings of every class of men accept, and that the opponents of the new Constitution admit in substance as readily as its friends. It must truly be acknowledged that, however they differ in other respects, they generally seem to agree in this view at least: our national system has serious imperfections, and something must be done to rescue us from impending anarchy. The facts behind this opinion are no longer matters for speculation. They have forced themselves on the feelings of the people at large. They have also wrung a reluctant admission from the very people whose mistaken policy did most to bring us to our present extremity. The admission is that these defects in the scheme of our federal government are real, defects which the intelligent friends of the Union have long pointed out and regretted.

issue: Source: "dreaded and detested by both; till mutual danger and mutual interest effected a union between them". "Both" = the sovereign and the common people. Candidate: "both dreaded and detested them. ... a union between them" -- the second "them" now reads as the barons (the "them" just before), so the referent of the union is wrong/unclear.
replacement: A sovereign of vigorous and warlike temper and superior abilities would gain a personal weight and influence that served, for a time, in place of a more regular authority. In general, however, the power of the barons triumphed over that of the prince. In many instances his dominion was thrown off entirely and the great fiefs were set up as independent principalities or States. In the instances where the monarch finally prevailed over his vassals, his success was chiefly owing to the vassals' tyranny over their dependents. The barons, or nobles, were equally the enemies of the sovereign and the oppressors of the common people, and were dreaded and detested by both. At length mutual danger and mutual interest brought about a union between the two that was fatal to the power of the aristocracy. If the nobles had instead kept the fidelity and devotion of their retainers and followers by acting with mercy and justice, their contests with the prince must almost always have ended in their favor, and in the reduction or overthrow of the royal authority.

issue: Source: "The Union here was far more intimate" (capital U as printed; STYLE-NOTE: "the Union" capitalized as printed). Candidate lowercases it: "Here the union was far closer". Restore as printed (judgment call: a lowercase "union" here is defensible for the Achaean league, but the table says keep the form as printed).
replacement: Here the Union was far closer, and the organization much wiser, than in the previous case. It will therefore appear that, though the league did not escape a similar catastrophe, it by no means deserved it as much.

issue: Source: the senate "had the sole and exclusive right of peace and war; of sending and receiving ambassadors; of entering into treaties and alliances; of appointing a chief magistrate or praetor". Candidate splits off "It also appointed a chief executive, called the praetor", so the "sole and exclusive right" no longer covers appointing the praetor, and "had the right of appointing" becomes a bare action. Keep it in the enumeration.
replacement: The cities that made up this league kept their municipal jurisdiction, appointed their own officers, and enjoyed perfect equality. The senate, in which they were represented, held the sole and exclusive right of peace and war, of sending and receiving ambassadors, of entering into treaties and alliances, and of appointing a chief executive, called the praetor, who commanded their armies. With the advice and consent of ten of the senators, the praetor not only administered the government while the senate was in recess but also had a great share in its deliberations when it was in session. Under the original constitution two praetors shared the administration, but after a trial a single one was preferred.

issue: Source: "The Achaeans, though weakened ... being joined by the AEtolians and Athenians, erected the standard of opposition" -- the AEtolians and Athenians join the Achaeans. Candidate: "they joined the AEtolians and Athenians and raised the standard", reversing who joined whom.
replacement: The Achaeans were now reduced to the dilemma of submitting to Cleomenes or begging aid from Macedon, their former oppressor. They chose the latter. The contests of the Greeks always gave that powerful neighbor a welcome chance to meddle in their affairs. A Macedonian army quickly appeared and Cleomenes was defeated. The Achaeans soon learned, as so often happens, that a victorious and powerful ally is only another name for a master. All that their most abject compliance could win from him was toleration of the exercise of their laws. Philip, now on the throne of Macedon, soon provoked fresh combinations among the Greeks by his tyrannies. The Achaeans were weakened by internal dissensions and by the revolt of Messene, one of their members. Even so, joined by the AEtolians and Athenians, they raised the standard of opposition. Finding themselves unequal to the undertaking even with this support, they once more resorted to the dangerous expedient of bringing in foreign arms. The Romans, to whom the invitation was made, eagerly accepted it. Philip was conquered and Macedon subdued. A new crisis followed for the league. Dissensions broke out among its members, and the Romans encouraged them. Callicrates and other popular leaders became paid instruments for luring their countrymen astray. To feed discord and disorder more effectively, the Romans had already proclaimed universal liberty(1) throughout Greece, to the astonishment of those who trusted their sincerity. With the same treacherous aims, they now drew the members away from the league by appealing to their pride over the violation it committed on their sovereignty. By these arts this union, the last hope of Greece, the last hope of ancient liberty, was torn to pieces. Such weakness and distraction were introduced that the arms of Rome found little difficulty in completing the ruin their arts had begun. The Achaeans were cut to pieces, and Achaia was loaded with chains, under which it groans to this hour.
